common_name: All Top Turnip (Rootless Cut-and-Come-Again Greens Turnip)

planting.note: Direct sow in late summer to early fall for a fall and winter greens crop, or in very early spring for a quick spring planting; in zone 9 Gulf South gardens, August-through-October sowings keep a steady cut-and-come-again harvest going well into winter.

directions: Direct sow thickly into fertile, loose soil in full sun and thin lightly, since All Top is grown purely for its leaves and forms little to no usable root. It is a classic Southern greens turnip, bred for a dense stand of large, smooth, deep green leaves rather than a marketable globe, and it regrows quickly after cutting, supporting repeated harvests from a single sowing rather than a one-time whole-plant pull. All Top matures fast — often ready to begin cutting in as little as 35 days — making it a dependable fast fall crop for gardeners who sowed other greens too late, and some seed catalogs note good tolerance to turnip mosaic virus. Harvest outer leaves regularly with scissors or a knife, leaving the center growing point intact, and expect sweeter flavor once leaves are touched by light frost.

common_name: Big Boy Purple Hull Cowpea (Texas Big Boy Southern Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed well past last frost; Big Boy is a long-podded purple hull southern pea valued for heavy yields of large, light tan peas packed into extra-long pods.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun once all frost danger has passed; Big Boy, also sold as Texas Big Boy, is a widely grown Southern purple hull pea prized for its unusually long pods, commonly eight inches or more, each packed with thirteen to sixteen large, light tan peas that give the variety its name and make shelling notably efficient for the yield. The semi-bush vines are heat- and drought-tolerant once established and, like other cowpeas, fix nitrogen in the soil, benefiting whatever crop follows. Harvest pods at the green shelling stage for fresh purple hull peas with excellent flavor, or let pods dry fully on the vine for a stored dry pea; pick regularly to keep plants setting new pods through the heat of summer.
sources: University of Florida/UF Seeds variety notes
